record.text: Scaled dot‑product attention takes a query vector, computes its dot product with each key vector to measure similarity, and then uses those scores (after a softmax) as weights to form a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors [S1][S3]. The dot products are divided by √d_k before the softmax because, when the dimensionality d_k is large, the raw dot products tend to have large magnitude (variance grows with d_k), which pushes the softmax into regions with very small gradients and makes learning difficult [S2]. Scaling by √d_k keeps the magnitude of the scores in a moderate range, preserving stable gradients for the softmax [S2]. This operation can be performed efficiently for many queries at once by packing Q, K, V into matrices and computing softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V [S1].

The positional encodings are added to the token embeddings and have the same dimension \(d_{\text{model}}\) so they can be summed; each encoding dimension is a sine or cosine function of the token’s position \(pos\) with wavelengths forming a geometric progression, specifically \(\text{PE}_{(pos,2i)}=\sin\!\big(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big)\) and \(\text{PE}_{(pos,2i+1)}=\cos\!\big(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big)\) [S1].  
The authors hypothesized that these sinusoidal functions let the model easily learn relative positions because a fixed offset \(k\) produces a linear transformation of the encoding [S1].  
Experiments showed that learned positional embeddings achieve nearly the same performance as the sinusoidal version [S2][S3].  
However, the sinusoidal scheme was preferred because it can generalize to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training, unlike learned embeddings [S3].

Moshi is full‑duplex because it does not rely on a single, turn‑based token stream; instead it models the user’s speech and the system’s speech as two parallel streams of semantic and acoustic tokens that are generated hierarchically in real time【S2】【S3】.  
By casting spoken dialogue as speech‑to‑speech generation, Moshi can listen and speak simultaneously, removing the need for explicit speaker‑turn segmentation and allowing overlapping speech, interruptions and interjections【S2】.  
The architecture uses a text‑language‑model backbone (Helium) together with a residual‑vector‑quantized neural audio codec (Mimi) to produce both streams of tokens in a streaming fashion, so each side’s audio is processed and generated concurrently【S3】.  
An “Inner Monologue” component predicts time‑aligned text tokens as a prefix to the audio tokens, which further enables streaming speech recognition while the model is still generating its own speech, supporting continuous bidirectional interaction【S4】.  
Thus Moshi’s dual‑stream token generation and hierarchical, time‑aligned processing give it the ability to handle both participants speaking at once with low latency【S3】【S4】.

record.text: Inner Monologue is a modeling paradigm in Moshi that treats text and audio as parallel token streams and introduces a controllable delay between them, allowing the language model to decide which modality drives generation [S3]. By setting the delay so that audio tokens are delayed relative to text tokens, the model can be forced to predict only text while using ground‑truth audio tokens, which yields a streaming Automatic Speech Recognition system with precise word‑level alignment [S3][S4]. Conversely, when the text tokens are delayed relative to audio tokens, the model generates audio conditioned on the already‑available text, producing a streaming Text‑to‑Speech system [S3][S4]. In practice the same trained Moshi model is used for both tasks; only the delay hyper‑parameter is changed, without any modification to loss, architecture, or training data [S1][S4]. For streaming TTS the audio tokens are delayed by 2 seconds during training, giving the model look‑ahead on text and allowing inference with teacher‑forced text tokens [S1]. For streaming ASR the text tokens are delayed by 2 seconds, letting the model listen to audio before emitting text and inference with teacher‑forced audio tokens [S1].

The encoder network first ingests the raw input, preserves fine‑grained details while compressing the sequence into richer “chunks” that are passed to the main network [S1][S4].  
The decoder network receives the upsampled output of the main network and combines those coarse‑grained representations with the fine‑grained residuals from the encoder to reconstruct information at the original scale [S1][S4].  
Both the encoder and decoder operate on the uncompressed, full‑resolution sequence (i.e., the original resolution before any down‑sampling) [S1][S4].

record.text:
The ratio loss is introduced to steer the model toward a target compression ratio, ensuring that the amount of data retained matches the desired level of compression while still preserving important content [S3].  
In the loss formulation, F denotes the actual fraction of vectors the model keeps, G represents the intended (target) compression fraction, and N is the total number of vectors in the sequence [S3].  
When F equals G, the loss reaches its minimum value of 1 (at F = G = N¹), indicating perfect adherence to the target ratio [S3].  
If F differs from G, the loss can theoretically drop below 1 (e.g., F = N¹+ε and G = N¹−ε), a behavior that is observed during training but still guides the model toward the correct ratio [S3].  
Because the routing module is encouraged to make confident (near‑binary) boundary decisions, F naturally converges toward G, making the ratio loss an effective regularizer for content‑adaptive compression [S3].  
Combined with the autoregressive prediction loss, this mechanism enables the model to learn which vectors to retain based on semantic importance rather than a fixed pattern [S3].
